terms.comment: Greek κύβος, with a short u. Vitruvius defines it as a body squared on every side with faces of equal width, which stays where it lands like the dice thrown on a gaming board. A child’s building block is a cubus too (see “building blocks”).

terms.gloss: a cube: Gellius’s Latin for κύβος
evidence: Gell. 1.20.3: quadrāta undique, quae … nōs “quadrantālia” dīcimus
terms.comment: Classically a liquid measure (eight congiī), a cubic foot; Gellius gives it as the Latin name of the solid.

evidence: Mart. 14.17.1: bis sēnō numerātur tessera pūnctō
terms.comment: The die of the gaming board, the everyday cube.

phrases.latin: Cubus sex latera habet, omnia quadrāta et paria.
phrases.english: A cube has six faces, all square and all the same.

phrases.latin: Is cum est jactus, quam in partem incubuit, dum est intāctus, inmōtam habet stabilitātem, utī sunt etiam tesserae quās in alveō lūdentēs jaciunt.
phrases.english: When it is thrown, it stays unmoved on whichever side it has fallen, as long as no one touches it, like the dice that players throw on the board.

sources: Lewis & Short: cubus · Lewis & Short: quadrantal · Lewis & Short: tessera
